entry.evidence: Here we extend the analysis to global scale by means of 25 years of AVISO altimetry data covering the (ice-free) global ocean.

sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML text with §-locators; PDF for figures)

steps.action: The authors take as given their own 2019 'vortex proxy' method, which rests on strong correlations between integrated kinetic energy and integrated enstrophy and was tested regionally in the California Current System.
steps.quote: the concept of a “vortex proxy” based on an observation of strong correlations

steps.action: They ask whether the proxy vortex representation works at global scale and gives reliable coarse-grained eddy statistics.
steps.quote: Here we extend the analysis to global scale by means of 25 years of AVISO altimetry data

steps.action: They take daily 0.25° AVISO absolute and anomaly geostrophic velocities (1993–2018) and compute KE, EKE and enstrophy. They note that EKE also reflects the meandering of the major currents.
steps.quote: enstrophy (the squared vorticity) is determined from the curl of the velocity field

steps.action: They adopt the Gaussian-shape hypothesis for mesoscale eddies from published SLA profile fits.
steps.quote: around 50 % of MEs are indeed well approximated by a Gaussian shape

steps.action: They recall the 2019 derivation for an isolated Gaussian vortex: I_EKE/I_Z = R_eff²/2. Strong correlation between the two integrals is expected when the Gaussian hypothesis holds (§2.3 ¶4).
steps.quote: When the time series of the two integrals are properly correlated, the ratio provides a key to estimate an effective size

steps.action: They choose the Pearson correlation coefficient between the time series of I_EKE and I_Z per tile.
steps.quote: we determined the Pearson correlation coefficient P by using the standard definition

steps.action: They check Pearson against Spearman rank correlation and find the two essentially identical (results not shown).
steps.quote: According to our tests, the two coefficients are essentially identical for the integrals

steps.action: They set three overlapping tilings (21×21, 11×11, 5×5 grid cells) with ocean-coverage thresholds near shorelines, instead of a detailed area analysis.
steps.quote: we will compare results for three different tilings: 21 × 21, 11 × 11, and 5 × 5 grid cells

steps.action: Numerical tests show that EKE time series at one location scale with the area ratio between tile sizes, but area normalization fails for Eq. (3).
steps.quote: Numerical tests prove that time series of EKE at a given location but at two different tile sizes are quite similar

steps.action: They reverse Eq. (3): census amplitudes are inserted to estimate the eddy kinetic energy per tile, which is compared with the directly computed EKE on the two larger tilings.
steps.quote: we reverse the consideration of Eq. () in order to get a hint about the partition of kinetic energy

steps.action: They take the linear beta-plane drift speed U_d = -βR_d² (as for long nondispersive Rossby waves) and the Chelton et al. (1998) gridded Rossby radii as the expectation for westward drift.
steps.quote: The simple formula for the drift speed is the same as for long nondispersive Rossby waves

steps.action: They design a time-lagged cross-correlation of I_EKE between zonally neighbouring tiles to estimate drift. For validation, zonal drift speeds are extracted from 2.76 million census tracks with the haversine formula.
steps.quote: We exploit this fact to estimate westward propagation velocities by evaluating the cross-correlation

steps.action: The global maps of Pearson P (Figure 2, p. 1366) are compared with the expected strong correlation. P is strong almost everywhere except in the 10° S–10° N band, and still significant (0.6–0.7) at 5×5 tiles.
steps.quote: The common feature is the strongly decreasing correlation in the latitude band 10 ∘ S–10 ∘ around the Equator.

steps.action: Across the three tilings, correlations are stronger for larger tiles, which matches the 2019 regional result.
steps.quote: indicates stronger correlations for larger tile sizes

steps.action: They estimate the effective proxy-vortex radius R_eff = sqrt(2 I_EKE/I_Z) globally (Figure 3, p. 1367); radii are anomalously large in the equatorial band.
steps.quote: The strong correlations permit giving an estimate for an effective proxy vortex radius R eff

steps.action: They compare zonal-mean R_eff from the three tilings with census equivalent radii (cyclonic and anticyclonic; Figure 4, p. 1367), masking tiles with no eddy centres. They also compare with the Rossby radius and with the Chelton et al. (2011) census.
steps.quote: The agreement between the five estimates of zonal mean effective radii R eff and R equiv is rather satisfactory

steps.action: They estimate the census eddy kinetic energy from stored amplitudes via Eq. (3) (Figure 5) and the tile-wise ratio I_EKE/EKE_ec (Figure 6). Local ratios range from 0.5 to 15, with a mean of about 6.2.
steps.quote: This approximation assumes that MEs have Gaussian sea level anomaly profiles in general.

steps.action: They compare the partition ratio with Amores et al. (2018), which is the same order of magnitude, and with their own 2019 regional value of about 2, which differs; they attribute the difference to the eddy-height estimate.
steps.quote: The range of mean ratios is of the same order of magnitude as found by

steps.action: They check zonal-mean ratios across medium and large tiles. They repeat all calculations with amplitudes shifted by +1 cm: the geographic tendencies hold, but the mean ratio drops from 6.2 to 4.3.
steps.quote: the partition ratio dropped to a mean value of 4.3 instead of 6.2

steps.action: They map the maximal cross-correlation and its lag (Figure 7, p. 1370). The lags show westward drift in 30° S–30° N and eastward drift in the ACC, Gulf and Kuroshio regions. Near-zero lags at the Equator and above 40° are tentatively linked to wind forcing.
steps.quote: indicating marked westward drift

steps.action: They compare zonal-mean drift speeds from cross-correlation with census track statistics and linear theory (Figure 8, p. 1370). Agreement holds in 5–30° on both hemispheres; discrepancies appear in 30–50° and in 5° S–5° N.
steps.quote: The results of the cross-correlation method are in good agreement with vortex tracking statistics

steps.action: To explain the discrepancies they propose rivals: EKE carried by coherent currents and gyre branches, equatorial baroclinic Rossby waves, and radiating long-lived eddies. None is tested.
steps.quote: mesoscale eddies are not the only form of kinetic energy transport on the ocean surfaces

steps.action: They inspect Hovmöller diagrams at 60° S, 31° N and 52° N (Figure 9, p. 1371). These show eastward ACC drift, the usual westward propagation, and a quasi-periodic giant Alaskan Stream ring (Figure 10).
steps.quote: we studied the Hovmöller diagrams (time–longitude plots) for several latitudes

steps.action: They retain the claim that the Gaussian proxy vortex approach works globally, validated against the eddy census.
steps.quote: We can shortly conclude that the original proposal by works on a global scale.

No; eddy size is inferred from an integral ratio under the Gaussian assumption
Characterize whether the proxy method works globally (sizes, energy partition, drift)
No rivals for the main claim; post hoc rivals (currents, Rossby waves, wind) for the drift discrepancies
No distinct predictions derived for the drift rivals
Conditions found: 25 years of global altimetry

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Yes: thousands of tiles and days, compared zonally against 64 million census eddies
Radii robust to tiling and metric; energy ratio sensitive to a 1 cm amplitude shift; drift agrees only in 5–30°
Kept: proxy vortex approach validated globally away from the Equator

end.claim: The Gaussian proxy-vortex method gives quick, reliable coarse-grained eddy statistics globally. Zonal-mean effective radii agree with a 64-million-eddy census outside 10° S–10° N, where the method breaks down.

decisive_move.sentence: The comparison of zonal-mean R_eff from three tilings with the census equivalent radii (Fig. 4) is what validates the proxy method globally; without it the radii are an unanchored ratio.

gates.evidence: The Gaussian hypothesis directed which quantities were computed (I_EKE, I_Z, their ratio) from archival AVISO data, but no new data were acquired (§2.3 ¶4). Correlations could have been weak, and R_eff could have disagreed with the census radii (§3.1 ¶1, §3.1 ¶4). Tilings, thresholds and lag filtering were not stated as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Pearson and Spearman rank correlation coefficients
Gaussian and steepness-parameter vortex solutions of the vorticity equation; enstrophy integrals
haversine formula for daily zonal travel distances
Python 3.6 with NumPy, SciPy and Basemap

limits: Sub-claims sit at different statuses. Zonal-mean R_eff is estimate_with_resolution outside ±10° (1σ bars for 21×21 only). The EKE partition ratio (about 6.2, or 4.3 with a +1 cm amplitude shift) is an estimate the authors call very sensitive. Drift speeds agree with tracking only in 5–30°. The explanations for the discrepancies (currents, Rossby waves, wind forcing, radiating eddies) are post hoc best explanations, not tested. The Spearman check, the tile-size EKE tests and the visual ellipse check are reported without results shown. Choices of tilings, the coverage thresholds (200/441, 80/121, 20/25) and lag filtering (τ = 0, 1, 2 d) are given without sensitivity results; that they were not pre-fixed is inference. Validation uses a census derived from the same AVISO data, so it is a method check, not independent data. Composition coded independent_replication because the authors re-derive their own 2019 regional result with new, global data against an external census. It is a self-generalization by the same group, not a replication by an independent team; none_fits is a defensible alternative. The paper was refereed (Uchida and one anonymous referee) and had an open discussion, but no review file was supplied, so the review sequence cannot be coded.

disagreements.target: Previous studies of the ratio of total to eddy kinetic energy
disagreements.support: The zonal-mean I_EKE/EKE_ec ratio is somewhat higher, though of the same order as Amores et al. (2018), and is sensitive to amplitude errors.
disagreements.quote: The ratio of total and eddy kinetic energies is somewhat higher than found in previous studies.

disagreements.target: Closed-contour eddy census (Faghmous et al. 2015) in the equatorial band
disagreements.support: Low-amplitude advected eddies in the gray zone are argued to be poorly detected and undersized by isocontours.
disagreements.quote: their detection by isocontours can have a large error and can easily result in underestimates of their size

disagreements.target: Ellipse fits of eddy shape in the census (Faghmous et al. 2015; Chen et al. 2019)
disagreements.support: A visual check of maps (not shown) suggests eddy isocontours have lobes and waves, so ellipses are an approximation.
disagreements.quote: a simple visual check of a couple of maps (not shown here) indicates that an ellipsoidal fit is also an approximation

disagreements.target: Treating geostrophic velocity anomalies as representing mesoscale eddies (e.g., Frenger et al. 2015; Ji et al. 2018)
disagreements.support: EKE maps show large contributions from meandering and relocation of major currents, shown by the overlap in Fig. 1.
disagreements.quote: partly reflects the activity of mesoscale eddies; however, it has significant contributions from the meandering

disagreements.target: Equating kinetic energy drift with eddy drift from vortex tracking and linear beta-plane theory
disagreements.support: Cross-correlation drift exceeds tracked eddy drift at higher latitudes; this is argued to come from currents, Rossby waves and other propagating features (Figs. 8, 9).
disagreements.quote: mesoscale eddies are not the only form of kinetic energy transport on the ocean surfaces

disagreements.target: The term 'super vortex' in Jánosi et al. (2019)
disagreements.support: The authors rename their own construct 'proxy vortex' to avoid overstatement.
disagreements.quote: here we rather use proxy vortex to avoid overstatement
